blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: This is the Annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for the FY 2019/20 which has been prepared in line with Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which require the Controller of Budget to submit to Parliament quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County Governments every four months. The report presents cumulatively budget performance for FY 2019/20.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the financial year, receipts into the consolidated fund amounted to Kshs.2.58 trillion , representing 97.8 per cent of the revised annual target of Kshs.2.65 trillion, a slight decline compared to Kshs.2.60 trillion received in the FY 2018/19. Total exchequer issues to MDAs, Consolidated Funds Service (CFS) and County Governments amounted to Kshs.2.53 trillion representing 92.5 per cent of the revised net estimates, a decline compared to 95.6 per cent recorded in the FY 2018/19. This comprised of Kshs.1.8 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.385.8 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.316 billion to the County Governments. Exchequer issues to counties comprised of Kshs.286.8 billion and Kshs.29.2 billion as equatable share and conditional grants respectively.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The total expenditure by National Government amounted to Kshs.2.53 trillion , representing 88.9 per cent of the revised gross estimates, a decline compared to 91.2 per cent recorded in the FY 2018/19. It comprised of development and recurrent expenditure of Kshs.614.3 billion (absorption rate of 86.2 per cent) and Kshs.1.9 trillion (89.8 per cent) respectively. Gross expenditure is higher than exchequer issues due to Apportions- in- Aid funding from Donors and Development Partners. Development expenditure recorded 13.6 per cent growth compared to Kshs.540.9 billion spent in the FY 2018/19. The highest development expenditure included; Capital Transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) of Kshs.346.3 billion, followed by Construction and Civil works at Kshs.92.5 billion, representing 56.4 per cent and 15 per cent of the gross development expenditure respectively.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Gross recurrent expenditure of Kshs.1.9 trillion comprised of Kshs.1.1 trillion which was incurred on MDAs recurrent programmes representing 87.8 per cent of the revised recurrent gross estimates and Kshs.807.3 billion towards Consolidated Fund Services representing 92.7 per cent of the revised estimates. This recorded a decline in the absorption of funds compared to FY 2018/19 when it recorded at 94.9 per cent and 95.7 per cent respectively. The decline in the absorption rate on recurrent expenditure is attributed to the interruption of planned activities for the financial year by the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in the second half of the FY 2019/20. Some of the key budget items highly affected by the pandemic recording low expenditure included Travelling, Training and Hospitality activities which are major spending lines by MDAs.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that a total of Kshs.445.6 billion was spent on Compensation to Employees representing 40 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs. The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) recorded the highest expenditure on compensation to employees at Kshs.254.6 billion translating to 23 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by the National Government MDAs attributed to the fact that the bulk of the TSC's budget is for teachers' salaries. The second highest expenditure item was current transfers to SAGAs at Kshs.303.8 billion, or 27.4 per cent of the total MDAs recurrent expenditure, recording a decline compared to Kshs.375.6 billion recorded in the FY 2018/19 representing 35.2 per cent of MDAs gross recurrent expenditure.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: In the FY 2019/20, Appropriations-in-Aid (A-I-A) reported by some MDAs amounted to Kshs.212.2 billion representing 78 per cent of the annual target of Kshs.273 billion. This comprised of Kshs.125.5
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: billion for development and Kshs.86.7 billion for the recurrent budget. Pending bills amounted to Kshs.53.49 billion, comprising of Kshs.33.54 billion for development and Kshs.19.95 billion for recurrent budget respectively. However, some MDAs did not report the A-I-A received and pending bills during the financial year which possibly resulted in understating of the actual A-I-A received and the position of the pending bill as at the end of the financial year.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The office of the Controller of Budget identified some of the key challenges that hindered effective budget implementation. These included; approval of Supplementary Budgets too close to the end of the financial year, therefore not allowing time for budget implementation and non-alignment of Supplementary Budgets to actual performance by MDAs resulting to a reduction below the level of expenditure already incurred. Others included delays in submission of budget performance reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget resulting in delay in reporting and consequently affecting budget oversight, high level of pending bills and Public debt, delay in release of exchequer and the negative economic effect of the COVID-19 pandemic.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The office of the Controller of Budget recommends that Supplementary Budgets should not be approved too close to year-end. The National Treasury should liaise with MDAs when effecting budget revisions to align reallocations to budget performance. Further, Accounting Officers should ensure timely submission of financial reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget in line with Section 83 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 to allow for timely preparation and publication of Budget Implementation Review Reports. Ministries, Departments and Agencies with pending bills should ensure their payments are prioritized as the first charge in the FY 2020/21 before embarking on new development projects. Finally, the office of the Auditor-General should conduct a special audit of the funds released towards COVID-19 pandemic interventions to give an assurance on value for money and whether the funds were utilized as required by the law.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: 1  INTRODUCTION
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya established the Office of the Controller of Budget with the mandate to oversee the implementation of the budgets of the National and County Governments by authorizing withdrawals from public funds under Articles 204, 206 and 207 of the Constitution and to report on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. This report fulfils the requirement of Article 228(6), of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 by presenting information on the budget implementation by National Government MDAs in the FY 2019/20.
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The report outlines budget performance by MDAs in FY 2019/20. It is organised into seven chapters. Chapter one offers an introduction. Chapter two provides a summary of receipts into the Consolidated Fund in the FY 2019/20. It also provides a breakdown on the disbursement of funds received into the Consolidated Fund to fund expenditure for MDAs, Consolidated Fund Services and to the fortyseven counties for both development and recurrent programmes.
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter three presents the overall budget performance. It presents summary performance for both development and recurrent expenditure by the MDAs and funds transferred to County Governments as shareable revenue and from Development Partners. It also presents Consolidated Fund Services performance which is discussed under recurrent expenditure. Consolidated Fund Services provides information on Public debt; Pensions and Gratuities; and Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders and Miscellaneous Services. The chapter also presents expenditure by economic classifications by the MDAs, for development and recurrent votes and identifies current and capital transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies.
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter four presents budget implementation by MDAs in the FY 2019/20 by analysing performance for both development and recurrent expenditure by Sectors. MDAs are classified into ten (10) Sectors according to the Classification of Functions of the Government. The Sectors are; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) (ii) Education (iii) Energy Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT) (iv) EWNR (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance Justice Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security and (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) and (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector.
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter five provides budget performance by programmes for each MDA and highlights programmes with the highest and lowest allocation in FY 2019/20. Chapter six highlights the issues that affected budget implementation in FY 2019/20 and provides recommendations aimed at improving budget implementation. Chapter seven provides a conclusion.
heading_path: 1  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The chapters are supported by annexes and a PDF version of the report is available on the COB website, https://cob.go.ke.

heading_path: 2.1 Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter provides a summary of receipts into the Consolidated Fund and analysis of exchequer issues to MDAs in the FY 2019/20. The exchequer issues are disaggregated into development, recurrent expenditure and to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 2.1 Introduction

blocks.text: 2.2 Analysis of Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2 Analysis of Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: This section presents a summary of the revenue estimates and receipts into the Consolidated Fund in the FY 2019/20. It also illustrates the trend of receipts into the Consolidated Fund over similar periods in the past five financial years.
heading_path: 2.2 Analysis of Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: 2.2.1 FY 2019/20 Revenue Estimates
heading_path: 2.2.1 FY 2019/20 Revenue Estimates

blocks.text: The revised revenue estimates for the FY 2019/20 was Kshs.2.7 trillion, an increase compared to Kshs.2.6 trillion budgeted in the FY 2018/19. To finance the budget, the national government through the National Treasury budgeted to raise funds from various sources which included: Tax revenue (Kshs.1.5 trillion), Non-tax revenue (Kshs.149.2 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.664.4 billion), External loans and grants Kshs.301.2 billion and other domestic financing at Kshs.54.3 billion.
heading_path: 2.2.1 FY 2019/20 Revenue Estimates

heading_path: 2.2.2 Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: In the FY 2019/20, total receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.2.6 trillion representing 97.8 per cent of the revised annual target. This amount comprised of cash from the previous financial year (FY 2018/19), Tax and Non-tax revenue, Domestic borrowing, External loans and grants and other domestic financing. blocks.text: 2.3 FY 2019/20 Overall Budget
heading_path: 2.3 FY 2019/20 Overall Budget

blocks.text: The revised gross estimates for the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.3.2 trillion. This comprised of Kshs.2.1 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.712.6 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.378.5 billion to County governments. blocks.text: 3.1 Introduction
heading_path: 3.1 Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter presents an overall budget performance in FY 2019/20. It presents summary performance for both development and recurrent expenditure by the national government Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs). The Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) is discussed under recurrent expenditure and provides information on Public debt; Pensions and Gratuities; and Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders and Miscellaneous Services. The chapter also presents expenditure by economic classifications by the national government entities, for development and recurrent votes respectively.

blocks.text: 3.3.1 Public Debt
heading_path: 3.3.1 Public Debt

blocks.text: The revised allocation towards repayment of public debt in FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.778.85 billion representing a decline of 8.2 per cent from Kshs.848.3 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. This allocation comprised of Kshs.532.5 billion and Kshs.253.35 billion for internal and external debt respectively. The internal debt comprised of Kshs.301.81 billion for interest payment and Kshs.223.68 billion for redemptions. On the other hand, external debt comprised of Kshs.131.87 billion towards payment of interest and Kshs.121.48 billion for redemption.
heading_path: 3.3.1 Public Debt

blocks.text: During the reporting period, actual expenditure on public debt was Kshs.717.65 billion. This amount represented 92.1 per cent of the revised gross estimates, which was a decline compared to 96.8 per cent (Kshs.821.3 billion) recorded in FY 2018/19. The decline is explained by the repayment of a commercial loan of USD.1 billion (Kshs.101,529 million) syndicated loan and USD.750 million (Kshs.77,722 million) debut international sovereign bond which matured in FY 2018/19.
heading_path: 3.3.1 Public Debt

blocks.text: As at 30th June 2020, the gross public debt stood at Kshs.6.69 trillion recording a 15.3 per cent growth compared to Kshs.5.80 trillion as at 30th June 2019. External debt grew by Kshs.492.67 billion while Domestic debt grew by Kshs.393.1 billion. The increases consisted of disbursements from multilateral organizations and uptake of domestic debt during the reporting period.
heading_path: 3.3.1 Public Debt

blocks.text: In the course of normal reviews during the financial year, OCOB noted that payment of management and commitment fees on loans that were yet to be disbursed long after execution of the loan agreements. Government procedure requires that project planning and approval should precede sourcing for funds, implying that borrowing can only be done when a programme or activity is already scheduled to commence. Therefore, continued payment of obligations on undisbursed loans is not prudent and does not meet any value for money considerations. .
heading_path: 3.3.1 Public Debt

blocks.text: 3.3.2 Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Services
heading_path: 3.3.2 Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Services

blocks.text: The revised allocation towards Salaries, Allowances and other miscellaneous services in FY 2019/20 was Kshs.4.64 billion, a decline of 30 per cent compared to Kshs.6.6 billion allocated in FY 2018/19. This comprised of payment of Salaries and Allowances for Constitutional Officeholders of Kshs.3.98 billion, Kshs.643.61 million towards payment of guaranteed debt and Kshs.15.5 million towards miscellaneous services.
heading_path: 3.3.2 Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Services

blocks.text: In FY 2019/20, total exchequer issues amounted to Kshs.3.3 billion representing 71.2 per cent of the revised gross estimates. Total expenditure towards this vote was Kshs.3.31 billion representing 71.4 per cent of the revised gross estimates. This comprised of Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders at Kshs.2.7 billion and Kshs.0.6 billion towards guaranteed loans to State Parastatals.
heading_path: 3.3.2 Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Services

blocks.text: The reduction in the expenditure for the period ended 30 th June 2020 compared to 30 th June 2019 was occasioned by vacancies in Constitutional Offices and other Commissions which expired and were not filled by close of the year despite a full budget provision. They include Controller of Budget, Auditor General, National Cohesion and Integration Commission, National Land Commission and Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission. Lastly, the demise of one Former President during the reporting period resulted into a reduction in the expenditure for former presidents.

blocks.text: In the FY 2019/20, travelling expenses recorded Kshs.14.6 billion comprising of Kshs.10.8 billion and Kshs.3.8 billion on domestic and foreign travel respectively. The decline is attributed to austerity measures on non-core activities and movement restriction both local and international to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 pandemic in the Country.
heading_path: 3.4.2.2 Operations and Maintenance (O&M)

blocks.text: Other O&M expenses which recorded a decline in the FY 2019/20 compared to previous FY 2018/19 include Hospitality at Kshs.6.4 billion compared to Kshs.9.8 billion, Training at Kshs.2.6 billion compared to Kshs.5.3 billion and Printing and Advertising at Kshs.1.9 billion compared to Kshs.4.3 billion respectively.

The decline in transfers to SAGAs is an effect of budget cuts to spending entities done to free money for core activities including COVID-19 associated expenses. heading_path: 3.5 Pending Bills for MDAs for the FY 2019/20

blocks.text: Pending bills are unsettled financial obligations at the end of the financial year that arise when an entity fails to settle invoiced amounts for goods and services properly procured and delivered. As of June 30th, 2020, fourty-four out of the total of seventy-one MDAs reported cumulative pending bills amounting to Kshs.53.49 billion. This amount comprised of Kshs.19.96 billion for recurrent and Kshs.33.54 billion for development pending bills. Seventeen MDAs had no pending bill as per the financial reports submitted to OCOB while ten MDAs failed to submit information on pending bills by the time of finalizing this report. blocks.text: 4  DEVELOPMENT AND RECURRENT EXPENDITURE ANALYSIS BY SECTOR
heading_path: 4  DEVELOPMENT AND RECURRENT EXPENDITURE ANALYSIS BY SECTOR

blocks.text: 4.1 Introduction
heading_path: 4.1 Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter presents budget implementation by MDAs in the FY 2019/20 by analysing performance for both development and recurrent expenditure by Sectors. MDAs are classified into ten (10) Sectors according to the Classification of Functions of the Government. The Sectors are discussed in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT), (iv) EWNR (EWNR), (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA), (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO), (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR), (x) SPCR Sector.
heading_path: 4.1 Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector
heading_path: 4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector

blocks.text: The sector consists of seven MDAs namely: Ministry of Lands and Physical Planning (MoLPP), State Department for Crop Development, Irrigation 1 , Agricultural Research, Livestock, Fisheries, Aquaculture and the Blue Economy and the National Land Commission (NLC). The sector has thirty-three (33) Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies and eleven (11) Training Institutions.
heading_path: 4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector

blocks.text: The sector is a major contributor to the 'Big Four' agenda on the achievement of 100 per cent food and nutrition security and provides broad opportunities on forward and backward linkages with other sectors of the economy such as manufacturing, distribution and other service-related industries. It is identified as a key sector that will drive delivery of the 10 per cent economic growth rate envisaged under the vision 2030 and accelerate attainment of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The sector plays a key role in the economic and social development of the country by enhancing employment and wealth creation, foreign exchange earnings, the security of land tenure and land management.
heading_path: 4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.72.4 billion representing 2.2 per cent of the revised gross national budget, an increase compared to Kshs.64.3 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The allocation comprised of Kshs.43.2 billion (60 per cent) for development and Kshs.29.2 billion (40 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Crop Development received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.37.2 billion equivalent to 51.3 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the National Lands Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.8 billion equivalent to 3 per cent of the total sector's allocation.

blocks.text: 4.3 Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3 Education Sector

blocks.text: The Education sector consists of five MDAs namely: State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education, University Education, Vocational and Technical Training, Post-Training and Skills Development and the Teachers Service Commission together with their affiliated agencies and institutions.
heading_path: 4.3 Education Sector

blocks.text: The Sector is committed to the provision of quality education, training, science, technology, research and skills development to all Kenyans. The Sector's overall goal is to increase access to education and training; improve quality and relevance of education; reduce inequality as well as leverage on knowledge and skills in science, technology, and innovation for global competitiveness. It also envisions contributing to the achievement of the 'Big Four Agenda' by providing the requisite skilled human resources and promoting research and development.
heading_path: 4.3 Education Sector

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.500.6 billion representing 15.5 per cent of the revised gross national budget, an increase compared to Kshs.460.4 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The allocation comprised of Kshs.21 billion (4 per cent) for development budget and Kshs.479.6 billion (96 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. TSC received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.256 billion equivalent to 51 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the State Department for Post Training and Skills Development had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.112.9 million.
heading_path: 4.3 Education Sector

blocks.text: TSC received the highest proportion of the Education Sector budget and this is attributed to its' key function of teacher resource management. Allocation to the State Department for Post Training and Skills Development is for the department's mandate on policy formulation for addressing the disconnect between demand and supply of skilled manpower and providing an institutional framework to devise and implement National, Sectoral and Workplace strategies to develop to improve the skills of the Kenyan workforce.

heading_path: 4.4 Energy,  Infrastructure  and  Information  Communications  Technology  (EI  & ICT) Sector

blocks.text: This sector consists of nine (9) MDAs namely; State Department for Infrastructure, Transport, Shipping and Maritime, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communications Technology, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Petroleum and the State Department for Energy.
heading_path: 4.4 Energy,  Infrastructure  and  Information  Communications  Technology  (EI  & ICT) Sector

blocks.text: The sector is a key enabler for sustained economic growth and government priorities and initiatives such as the Big 4 Agenda. In the medium term, the sector aims at sustaining and expanding infrastructural facilities to support a rapidly growing economy in line with the priorities contained in the Medium-Term Plan (MTP III) and Vision 2030.
heading_path: 4.4 Energy,  Infrastructure  and  Information  Communications  Technology  (EI  & ICT) Sector

blocks.text: The key strategic goals of the sector are to develop and maintain sustainable services to facilitate the efficient movement of goods and people, develop and sustain access to opportunities in the shipping and maritime industry, improve universal access to information technology-enabled services and to improve access to a competitive, reliable and safe supply of petroleum products to all Kenyans, among others.
heading_path: 4.4 Energy,  Infrastructure  and  Information  Communications  Technology  (EI  & ICT) Sector

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.470.2 billion representing 14.6 per cent of the revised gross national budget, an increase compared to Kshs.443.7 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The allocation comprised of Kshs.381.2 billion (81 per cent) for development budget and Kshs.89.1 billion (19 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Infrastructure received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.240.1 billion equivalent to 51 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the State Department for Shipping and Maritime had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.2 billion equivalent to 0.4 per cent of the total sector's allocation.

heading_path: 4.5 Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: The EWNR Sector consist of four MDAs namely: Environment and Forestry, Water and Sanitation, Mining and the State Department for Wildlife.
heading_path: 4.5 Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: The overall goal of this sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment. Its specific objectives are to: provide policy, legal and integrated framework for sustainable management of the environment and natural resources towards socio-economic development and enhance capacity building for environment, water and natural resources management. It also aims at increasing utilization of land through irrigation, drainage and land reclamation, enhance research on environment, water and natural resources for sustainable development, protect and reclaim the environment in order to establish a durable and sustainable system of development and resilience to climate change.
heading_path: 4.5 Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.85.3 billion representing 2.6 per cent of the revised gross national budget, an increase compared to Kshs.72.8 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The allocation comprised of Kshs.60.9 billion for development budget representing 71 per cent of the sector's total allocation and Kshs.24.4 billion for recurrent budget representing 29 per cent of the sector's allocation. The Ministry of Water and Sanitation received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.61 billion equivalent to 71.5 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the State Department for Mining had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.0.9 billion (1.1 per cent) of the total sector's allocation.

heading_path: 4.6 General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) Sector

blocks.text: The General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of six MDAs, namely the State Departments for Industrialization, Co-operatives, Trade, East African Community, Regional and Northern Corridor Development and Tourism.
heading_path: 4.6 General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) Sector

blocks.text: The sector is a significant player in job and wealth creation, industrial development, investments and promotion of trade, tourism development, savings mobilization and cooperative development, regional integration and regional development.

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.33.6 billion representing 1 per cent of the revised gross national budget, a decrease compared to Kshs.34 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. heading_path: 4.7 Governance, Justice, Law and Order Sector (GJLO)

blocks.text: The GJLO Sector comprises of fifteen MDAs which include: State Department for Interior, State Department for Correctional Services, State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services, State Law Office and Department of Justice, The Judiciary, Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC), Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Office of the Registrar of Political Parties, Witness Protection Agency (WPA), Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), Judicial Service Commission (JSC), National Police Service Commission (NPSC), National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC), and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA).
heading_path: 4.7 Governance, Justice, Law and Order Sector (GJLO)

blocks.text: The sector implements the following functions; provision of security, correctional services, legal advisory services to government agencies and administration of justice. It also plays a major role in promoting integrity and the fight against corruption, provision of prosecution services, regulating political parties, protecting witnesses and human rights. Further, the sector plays an instrumental role in the delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, inclusion of marginalized groups and communities and civilian policing oversight.
heading_path: 4.7 Governance, Justice, Law and Order Sector (GJLO)

blocks.text: Other functions include; border management, peacebuilding and conflict management, registration services, regulation of the gaming industry, provision of population management services, eradication of drugs and substance abuse, crime research and government printing services.
heading_path: 4.7 Governance, Justice, Law and Order Sector (GJLO)

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.208.5 billion representing 6.5 per cent of the revised gross national budget, a slight increase compared to Kshs.207.9 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The allocation comprised of Kshs.13 billion (6 per cent) for development budget and Kshs.195.5 billion (94 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Interior received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.135.5 billion equivalent to 65 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.397 million (less than 1 per cent) of the total sector's allocation.

blocks.text: 4.8 Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8 Health Sector

blocks.text: The Health Sector is responsible for the provision and coordination of the health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery and regulation and control of health care. The Sector comprises of Ministry of Health and seven Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies namely; Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH), Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital (MTRH), Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), Kenya Medical Supplies Authority (KEMSA), Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC), National AIDS Control Council (NACC), and the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF).
heading_path: 4.8 Health Sector

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in FY 2019/20 was Kshs.119.9 billion representing 29.6 per cent of the gross national budget, representing an increase from Kshs.92.5 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. This allocation comprised of Kshs.43.8 billion (36.5 per cent) for development expenditure and Kshs.76.1 billion (63.5 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The significant increase in allocation when compared to FY 2018/19 is mainly due to the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, which precipitated the need for government to provide additional financial resources through the Ministry of Health for interventions by both the national and county governments.
heading_path: 4.8 Health Sector

blocks.text: Additional funds were availed to the following hospitals; KNH, Mbagathi District, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral, MTRH, Kitui and Mandera General Hospital. Other interventions included; implementation of the Kenya Emergency Response Project which was allocated Kshs.5.35 billion, conversion of a day care centre to a COVID-19 wards for patients at KNH at a cost of Kshs.140 million, operationalization of 300 bed capacity at Kenyatta University Teaching Referral and Research Hospital at a cost of Kshs.526.5 million and cash transfer to counties amounting Kshs.7.71 billion, among others.

heading_path: 4.9 National Security Sector

blocks.text: The Sector comprises the Ministry of Defence and the National Intelligence Service (NIS). blocks.text: 4.10  Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) Sector
heading_path: 4.10  Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) Sector

blocks.text: The Public Administration and International Relations(PAIR) Sector consists of 16 MDAs namely; The Presidency, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, National Treasury, State Department for Planning; Devolution, Public Service, State Department Youth, Parliamentary Service Commission, National Assembly, Parliamentary Joint Services, Commission on Revenue Allocation, Public Service Commission, Salaries and Remuneration Commission, Auditor General, Controller of Budget, and The Commission on Administrative Justice.
heading_path: 4.10  Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) Sector

blocks.text: The sector provides overall policy direction and leadership to the country, oversees national legislation as well as the human resource function in the public service. It further coordinates national policy formulation, implementation, resource mobilization, allocation and management, devolution oversight, coordinating the implementation of youth policy and mainstreaming in national development, implementation of Kenya foreign policy, and oversight on the use of public resources and service delivery.

blocks.text: The revised budgetary allocation to the sector in the FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.251.8 billion representing 7.8 per cent of the revised gross national budget, an increase compared to Kshs.225.9 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. The National Treasury received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.78 billion equivalent to 31 per cent of the sector's total allocation while the Commission on Revenue Allocation had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.364.7 million (less 1 per cent ) of the total sector's allocation.

blocks.text: 6  KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
heading_path: 6  KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: 6.1 Introduction
heading_path: 6.1 Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter highlights issues that affected budget implementation in FY 2019/20. Further, it provides recommendations aimed at improving budget implementation to achieve effective budget execution.
heading_path: 6.1 Introduction

blocks.text: 6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations
heading_path: 6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations

blocks.text: In the course of overseeing budget implementation, the OCOB identified the following key issues which affected budget implementation in the FY 2019/20.
heading_path: 6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations

blocks.text: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance
heading_path: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance

blocks.text: Budget revision through Supplementary budgets is permissible under Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 44 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012. Budget revision is necessary to rationalize budgetary allocations to non-core activities to release resources for pressing budget needs. Timing of Supplementary Budgets, however should allow time for MDAs to implement the planned activities.
heading_path: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance

blocks.text: In FY 2019/20, the National Treasury submitted Supplementary Budget I, II and III for approval by Parliament, which mainly rationalized budgetary allocations for non-core activities to release resources for COVID-19 Pandemic interventions and implementation of development activities. The third Supplementary Budget was assented to on 30 th June 2020. As a result, implementing entities did not have adequate time to implement budget activities benefiting from budget revisions. While the budget revision was necessary, some budget performance information such as exchequer issues and incurred expenditure were not considered. As a result, we noted reduction of some budget provisions below the level of expenditures already incurred.
heading_path: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance

blocks.text: The National Treasury should liaise with MDAs before effecting budget revisions to appropriately align budget allocations to actual performance. Supplementary Budgets should be prepared in good time to allow Parliament to consider and approve them in good time for timely budget implementation.
heading_path: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance

blocks.text: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget
heading_path: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget

blocks.text: Article 228 (6) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of budgets of the national and county governments every four months. The Controller of Budget's report is based on quarterly reports on financial and non-financial performance submitted by MDAs in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012.
heading_path: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget

blocks.text: During the year, the office noted delays in submission of the quarterly performance reports by some MDAs, causing subsequent delays in reporting and consequently affected the level of oversight of budget implementation by Parliament and other stakeholders.
heading_path: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget

blocks.text: The Accounting Officers should submit their financial and non-financial performance reports to the OCOB within fifteen days following the end of each quarter in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012 to facilitate timely reporting on budget implementation.
heading_path: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget

blocks.text: 6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills
heading_path: 6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills

blocks.text: As at 30 th June 2020, MDAs reported pending bills stood at Kshs.53.5 billion. From an analysis of reports received from MDAs, pending bills have been attributed to late submission of invoices and completion certificates by merchants by the end of the financial year, contested Court awards, historical cases and delays in release of exchequer issues, among others.
heading_path: 6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills

blocks.text: We recommend all MDAs with pending bills ensure their payments are prioritized as a first charge in the budget implementation cycle for the FY 2020/21 before embarking on other new projects.
heading_path: 6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills

blocks.text: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic
heading_path: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic

blocks.text: The first COVID-19 case in Kenya was confirmed in mid-March 2020, prompting the government to institute stringent measures to curb the spread of the disease. While the COVID-19 pandemic is primarily a health crisis with far-reaching economic ramifications, the responses instituted to control its spread have disrupted millions of livelihoods with a disproportionate impact on poor households and the global economic environment.
heading_path: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic

blocks.text: Given the disruptions occasioned by the actions taken by the government to contain the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic, it is clear that the measures have impacted on all sectors of the economy. In addition, it affected MDAs planned activities resulting in low expenditure of some budget items. These included Travelling, both domestic and foreign, Training and Hospitality.
heading_path: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic

blocks.text: The OCOB recommends that there is a need for continuous monitoring and reviewing the instituted measures on the impact to the economy by respective institutions to advice promptly on a framework for action aimed at saving lives, protecting households, businesses, and the economy from the possible decline caused by the pandemic.
heading_path: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic

blocks.text: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds
heading_path: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds

blocks.text: The first COVID-19 case was confirmed in Kenya in mid-March 2020, prompting the Government to introduce stringent measures to curb its spread. The government received funds from donors and other Development Partners which were then set aside through the Ministry of Health funds toward COVID-19 interventions. The purposes of the funds included operationalization of COVID-19 centres, increasing bed capacity at referral hospitals, provision of personal protective equipment to health workers and cash transfer to the Counties, among other interventions.
heading_path: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds

blocks.text: Some of the programmes funded through Ministry of Health included the Kenya Emergency Response Project (Kshs.5.35 billion), conversion of  a daycare centre to a ward for COVID-19 patients at KNH at Kshs.140 million, operationalization of 300 bed capacity at Kenyatta University Teaching Referral and Research Hospital at Kshs.526.5 million and cash transferred to counties at Kshs.7.71 billion, among others.
heading_path: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds

blocks.text: The expenditure on COVID-19 pandemic interventions is yet to be audited and the OCOB recommends that the office of the Auditor-General conducts special audits to give an assurance on the value for money and whether the funds were utilized for the intended purpose as required by law.
heading_path: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds

blocks.text: 6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases
heading_path: 6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: Analysis of financial reports submitted to the OCOB by MDAs revealed that some MDAs expenditures were higher than the exchequer releases for the period, especially on development budget. This was partly due to Appropriations-in-Aid, funding from Donors and Development partners which were not released as exchequers through the Consolidated Fund but received directly to MDAs projects and activities as approved in their budget. This appears to be contrary to Article 206 (1) of the Constitution which specifies that, all government revenues should be received in the Consolidated Fund.
heading_path: 6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: The OCOB recommends review of the law which allows MDAs to spend funds before they have been received in the Consolidated Fund as this will enhance transparency and accountability.
heading_path: 6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases
heading_path: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: In FY 2019/20, the total exchequer issues to National and County Governments was Kshs.2.53 trillion, representing 92.5 per cent of the annual revised net estimates. This was a decrease compared to 95.6 per cent recorded in the FY 2018/19 (Kshs.2.50 trillion in absolute figures). It would be expected that by the end of the financial year, the exchequer releases should be at 100 per cent of the annual estimates.
heading_path: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: From the analysis of reports submitted by the MDAs, the low level of expenditure, as well as the pending bills at the end of the year, would be attributable to delays in exchequer releases by the National Treasury. County governments received Kshs.316 billion (91 per cent of the revised net estimates) and this comprised of Kshs.286.8 billion as equitable share and Kshs.29.2 billion as conditional grants. As a result, the equitable share to the counties for June 2020 was not disbursed and was only released in FY 2020/21.
heading_path: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: Delay in the release of exchequers delays the implementation of the activities planned by MDAs and Counties and subsequently affects the timely delivery of services. The OCOB recommends that the National Treasury releases funds to the MDAs based on their annual work-plans and cash flow projections. Funds to counties should be released in accordance to Section 17(6) of the PFM Act, 2012 which states that the National Treasury shall at the beginning of every quarter and in any event not later than the fifteenth day from the commencement of the quarter disburse monies to county governments.
heading_path: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases

blocks.text: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: As at 30th June 2020, the gross public debt stood at Kshs.6.69 trillion and grew by 15.3 per cent compared to Kshs.5.80 trillion as at 30th June 2019. Disaggregation by External and Internal debt reveals that the former grew by Kshs.492.67 billion while latter grew by Kshs.393.1 billion. Despite the growth in the total loan portfolio, there was a decline in repayment compared to FY 2018/19 when two commercial loans amounting to Kshs.179.3 billion became due.
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: Actual expenditure of public debt amounted to Kshs.717.65 billion in FY 2019/20, representing 92.1 per cent of the revised gross estimates and 45.6 per cent of the ordinary revenue for the year.
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: Review of the external debt payments revealed instances where the government continued to pay regular loan commitment and management fees for loans that were yet to be disbursed long after execution of loan agreements. The continued payment of obligations on undisbursed loans is not
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: prudent and does not meet value for money considerations. The Government is obliged to ensure that its financing needs and payment of obligations are met at the lowest possible cost in the market and uphold the spirit of Article 201(d) of the Constitution which requires prudent and responsible use of public money.
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: Accordingly, OCOB recommends that, the National Treasury and Planning should undertake an analysis of all loans to identify those that are yet to be disbursed long after execution of the loan agreements. These should be reassessed if still required and appropriate action taken in order to reduce payments on the undisbursed loans
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt

blocks.text: 7  CONCLUSION
heading_path: 7  CONCLUSION

blocks.text: The Office of the Controller of Budget prepared this Annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report covering the period July 2019 to June 2020 in fulfilment of Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016. The report sought to provide information on budget implementation in FY 2019/20 and identified key issues that hampered effective budget execution by the National Government.
heading_path: 7  CONCLUSION

blocks.text: In FY 2019/20, the revised gross budget for the national government was Kshs.3.22 trillion recording a slight growth compared to Kshs.3.12 trillion recorded for the FY 2018/19. Receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.2.58 trillion which was 97.8 per cent of the annual target, a slight decline compared to Kshs.2.6 trillion received in the FY 2018/19 (99.4 per cent of the annual target). The decline could be attributable to the effect of some measures introduced by the government towards improving disposable income to the citizens to curb adverse effects COVID-19 pandemic like tax reduction on Value Added  Tax and Pay as You Earn, among others. The total exchequer issues in the financial year were Kshs.2.53 trillion representing 92.5 per cent of the revised net estimates. This comprised of Kshs.385.75 billion for development expenditure, Kshs.1.83 trillion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.316 billion towards county governments representing 87.7 per cent, 93.9 per cent and 90.8 per cent respectively. However,  the equitable share to counties for the month of June, 2020 from the National Government was not released and was carried forward to FY 2020/21.
heading_path: 7  CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Total expenditure for the national government was Kshs.2.53 trillion representing an overall budget absorption rate of 88.9 per cent, a decline compared to the 91.2 per cent achieved in the FY 2018/9. This comprised of development expenditure of Kshs.614.3 billion, an absorption rate of 86.2 per cent and recurrent expenditure of Kshs.1.92 trillion, representing 89.8 per cent of the revised gross recurrent budget. The decline in the absorption rate could be attributable to interruption of planned activities for the MDAs by budget cuts to set aside funds towards COVID -19 pandemic and the control measures put in place to curb its spread in the Country.
heading_path: 7  CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Despite the resilience of the economy to the global effect of the economic environment caused by the spread COVID-19, there is a need to address some of the key issues the office of the Controller of Budget identified as hampering overall budget implementation to deliver on the country's development agenda. These include the timing and aligning of the Supplementary Budget to actual performance, stemming of high pending bills and mitigating the economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The National Treasury should liaise with Ministries, Departments and Agencies before effecting budget revisions and ensure Supplementary Budgets are prepared in good time and approved by Parliament in time to allow the timely implementation of the budget. MDAs with pending bills should ensure their payments are prioritized as the first charge in the next budget before embarking on new development projects. Delay in the release of exchequers delays the implementation of the activities planned by MDAs and Counties and subsequently affects the timely delivery of services. The National Treasury and Planning releases funds to the MDAs based on their annual work-plans and cash flow projections. Funds to counties should be released in accordance to Section 17(6) of the PFM Act, 2012. We recommend the office of the Auditor-General to conducts audits of the funds released towards COVID-19 pandemic interventions to give an assurance on value for money and whether the funds were utilized as required by the law.
heading_path: 7  CONCLUSION
